📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’re in a great era for affordable fashion-collab watches. Timex is leading the way: its link-ups with Noah, Todd Snyder, and J. Crew are masterclasses in adding personality to classic designs without going OTT. But don’t count Casio out of the race. The Japanese giant has just followed up its 2024 collab with APC. The pair are perfectly matched: Casio watches are known for being beautifully functional and understated—adjectives that fit APC’s spartan aesthetic too.

The first collaboration between the two brands saw them rework the hallowed A1000 digital-display watch. That release stripped back a lot of the original’s markings and added the APC logo on the dial. This time around, it's the AQ-240 getting a makeover. The case is squarer than the rectangular A1000, and while there’s a narrow window for a digital display, the watch maintains the traditional analog format with hands and hour markers. Here, you get the best of both worlds. The watch is sold out on APC's website but still available through Casio, so act fast if you want one. The silver variant is $110, and the gold goes for $135.

According to recent reports, what about the APC-ness of it all? That part is the opposite of loud: as with the previous collab, there isn’t much giving away the brand's participation. We’ve got the APC logo on the dial and the buckle, plus the brand’s guitar-and-dagger insignia engraved out of sight on the caseback. Casio already offers the regular A1000 in a bunch of different colorways, but these two fresh ones are made specifically for the APC collab. The release includes a silver case with a dark-green dial and another in gold on gold. Both of the pieces have a brushed sun-ray effect on the dial. The vibe is refined and stripped back; this is a fashion watch that almost feels anti-fashion.

Sources indicate that maybe the best way to think about it is as the reverse side of the coin to the excellent latest G-Shock 2500 Series. Both come from Casio, and both are minimal and functional. But the G-Shocks are massive and bulky, with a design that seems to tip its hat to Patek Philippe’s Nautilus. These new ones are slim and nearly dressy. Put the two new releases together, and you’ve got pretty much all bases covered. And if those aforementioned Timex collabs felt a bit too classicist for you, then the Casio-APC partnership takes things in a more modern direction. Far from just being a cash grab, the “fashion watch” is now one of the best routes into affordable, on-point horology.

I Am the Wildest Dream of Every Black and Brown Trans Woman Before Me

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As an influencer, a lot of times I'm the only trans person—or the only trans person of color—in the room.
  • That’s especially true in this current political and cultural climate.
  • It’s been particularly challenging, too, as a trans person in the public eye; there's been many instances where my safety has been jeopardized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As an influencer, a lot of times I'm the only trans person—or the only trans person of color—in the room. It’s a lot of pressure, and there have been times where I have anxiety before going to certain spaces because I will question "Do I belong here?" But I’ve learned that that’s just the patriarchy and society trying to make us feel like we're not worthy.

That’s especially true in this current political and cultural climate. The trans community, especially the Black and brown trans community, gets so much hate—that’s why I’m very offended when people say being trans “is a choice.” Like, living with and navigating these stigmas and mistreatments isn't something that someone would willing choose.

It’s been particularly challenging, too, as a trans person in the public eye; there's been many instances where my safety has been jeopardized. When I get looked at, I'm thinking, They're looking at me either because I'm pretty or because I'm a viral trans person online. The differentiator is literally if I'm being chased home, which has happened multiple times. Since I speak out for trans women that can't speak for themselves, I'm also putting myself at risk. But at the same time, I think I can also make it safer for the next girl down the line.

According to recent reports, it's so rewarding being that person others can look up to. I love reassuring other trans women that they can do certain things or just live their lives authentically, loud, and open. But sometimes I'm like, Oh my god, how nice and easy would it be for me to just be silent and be in the background? But I don't think I was born to be a background girl. I'm front and center.

Sources indicate that and I think that the trans women before me would want me to be. The hard work that those women put for girls like me now, I have to show up for that. I think about trans women on the front lines of trans rights, like Marsha P. Johnson or Sylvia Rivera—they were front and center at Stonewall. They were the voices for many then, and there was so much more violence. The community was pretty much hidden at the time, too.

There's so much trans history lost, and Trans Day of Remembrance resurfaces those stories. A lot of times things get pushed under the rug because trans people are seen as not crucial to the media, or people in general, especially after all the propaganda that's been pushed out by certain administrations. But every year on this day, I learn about a different girl, especially outside of the U.S. I’ve learned so much about how some surgeries started because certain trans women needed gender-affirming care, and they paved the way for girls down the line.

Education is the number one thing. I want people to know that your understanding of trans identities is not what you think and that there's a lot more to learn. There are times when I get frustrated because I see the stigmas and the rhetoric online that's really just misinformation, rumors, and lies that people make up about trans people. A lot of trans women have died because that ignorance can lead to trans violence. It's really sad to see. But we made it back then—and it was hard then—so we'll make it now. We're a strong community.

The trans community, we show up for ours (for the most part). There's a couple spaces made for Black trans queer people, like the Black Trans Kitchen by Queen Jean—it’s really beautiful. And Gia Love created the annual Celebration of Black Trans Women Cookout. Trans women that make spaces like that really inspire me because they remind our community that we matter. And we as trans people need spaces where we can just be ourselves, and really show care to one another. Those spaces not only keep me humble, but also remind me of everything I've been through. It makes me feel so grateful and privileged to be alive today because a lot of girls don't make it.

In a recent development, with the work that I do and everything I create, I want other trans women to see me and know that they belong and that they can be in those spaces too. I want to see more, especially more trans women of color, in positions of power and in rooms where you rarely ever see them.

In a recent development, I hope other trans women see that they can be their most authentic self, and that they can feel confident regardless of what anybody claims. If you believe you're an amazing, beautiful person, it will reflect on the outside. I want people to feel that way and do that inner work because it's important, especially for our survival as trans people.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last night, Taylor Swift made her grand return to the Country Music Awards. Taking the award show’s stage for the first time since 2013, the singer-songwriter performed a mashup of her Single of the Year-nominated Toy Story 5 track, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” and one of her OG country classics: “Our Song.” Released in 2006 as the third single off her debut, self-titled album, the song choice was an emotional tribute to her Nashville origins—reminding the crowd that before she was touring the world as a global pop star, she was writing lyrics in math class and knocking on the doors of Music Row to try to get a record deal.

But the inclusion of “Our Song” wasn’t the only nod to her roots. Throughout the performance, which followed Swift from a backstage dressing room through the Bridgestone Arena hallways and eventually to the stage, the Easter egg professional sprinkled in many references to her early days. And the Swifties are convinced the hints might mean a re-recorded version of her debut album is on its way. (When announcing she bought her masters in May 2025, Swift revealed that she had already recorded an entire “Taylor’s Version” of her first record—though she has been quiet about it ever since.).

Ahead, we break down all the Easter eggs you might have missed from Swift’s CMAs performance.

When the performance kicked off, we saw Swift getting ready in a dressing room backstage. At first glance, the whole place was covered in dresses—with several gowns draped on the plush couch and even more hung on a clothing rack. But once we looked closely, we realized that each of the pieces came from the star’s archive. There was the BCBG halter-neck dress worn to the 2006 Academy of Country Music Awards (ACMs), the sea foam-green maxi from the “Teardrops on My Guitar” music video, and, most notably, the champagne beaded Sandi Spika gown worn to the artist’s first CMAs. It was here that Swift was awarded with the 2007 Horizon Award at the age of 17, definitively declaring it to be the “highlight of [her] senior year.”.

It has been revealed that from the dressing room, Swift walked through the arena hallways, interacting with a handful of other artists (see here)—from Eric Church to Rascal Flatts to Sugarland to Keith Urban. Every person she encountered she had either opened for, collaborated with, or had a connection to from her early days. One exception was Lainey Wilson—making people guess that the country musician might be featured on the (unconfirmed) forthcoming re-record.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Chic, playful, holiday”: This is how Amelia Gray sums up H&M Studio Holiday 2026, a collection that makes a case for getting dressed with a little more imagination. The model, who is at the moment one of the industry’s most recognizable faces, knows a thing or two about making an outfit memorable. These days, though, her approach is taking a more refined turn. “My personal style right now is definitely elevating, becoming more mature, chicer, and more refined,” she says. “I think H&M’s collection reflects that perfectly.”.

Like she notes, that evolution feels right at home with H&M Studio. The brand’s most directional offering, Studio collections bring a more experimental perspective to the tech giant’s portfolio, with limited-edition designs developed by the Stockholm atelier’s in-house team. For holiday 2026, the inspiration comes from the theatrical world of early-1900s Paris, where grand opera houses and salons set the scene for expressive dressing. Sweeping proportions, tactile fabrics, and unexpected details give the collection a sense of movement, while sharp tailoring keeps things grounded. The result is a wardrobe that feels equally suited to a festive gathering and an ordinary day that calls for something special.

Gray has already picked her favorite combination. “I loved the bomber jacket with the dress,” she states. “That outfit is great for Thanksgiving or Christmas dinner.” The bomber jacket, finished with a fluffy collar, brings a relaxed edge to the dual-fabric dress, which has a full balloon skirt that gives the look plenty of movement. Fluffy-lined ballet flats complete the outfit and add a sense of playfulness. Together, the pieces strike a balance between dressed-up and laid-back.

In a recent development, the bomber also has plenty of mileage beyond the dinner table. Gray calls it her “new favorite,” and for good reason: “The bomber jacket is perfect to dress up and down. With jeans. With a skirt. With shorts.” Throw it over denim for a casual weekend lunch, or pair it with a sleek pencil for a night out. The trick is to let the contrast do the work. A sporty jacket can change the mood of a dress, just as a more polished piece can bring an unexpected finish to something casual.

It has been revealed that some moments call for a dress that handles the styling decisions for you. The satin open-shoulder dress does exactly that, bringing a fluid and elegant neckline to the occasion. Its silhouette has enough presence to stand on its own, while dangle hoop earrings add movement and a touch of shine. It’s an easy combination for a holiday party, a dinner reservation, or any invitation that warrants getting dressed up without spending an hour figuring out what to wear.

The key is to keep the rest of the look uncomplicated. The dress could also take on a different personality with a more casual shoe or a relaxed jacket layered over it. That’s part of the appeal of a versatile occasion piece: It doesn’t have to be saved for one particular night on the calendar.

A peplum top and an A-line skirt make an interesting study in proportion. The puff sleeves and defined waist of the top bring shape up above, while the viscose skirt creates a fluid counterpoint below. It’s a combination that feels polished without being overly formal—a smart option for a lunch that turns into an afternoon of shopping or a dinner with friends. For a slightly more understated take, swap in the scoop-neck viscose top. The silhouette becomes simpler, but the skirt still gives the outfit its sense of movement.

Sources indicate that the handbag adds another layer of personality. Its soft shape, velvet rope handle, and oversize tassel bring texture and a hint of old-world theatricality to the mix, tying back to the collection’s Parisian inspiration. It’s also the kind of accessory that can change the feel of classic pieces, whether carried with a coordinated outfit or used to add interest to a simple top-and-jeans combination.

A crisp cotton poplin shirt is one of those wardrobe staples that rarely needs an introduction. Here, its clean lines meet the texture and embellishment of an embroidered crepe skirt, creating a combination that feels easy to wear. Over-the-knee leather boots round out the outfit, giving it a little more attitude. It’s a strong look for a holiday gathering, a night at the theater, or a dinner when your denim go-to simply won’t do. For another interpretation, the skirt can be swapped for barrel-leg trousers, while a raw-edged puff-sleeve blouse offers an alternative to the cotton poplin.

In a recent development, the appeal lies in the mix of familiar and fashion-forward pieces. A poplin shirt is hardly an adventurous purchase, but paired with a more expressive skirt and statement boots, it takes on a different character. This balance also makes the individual pieces easier to wear beyond the occasion. The shirt works with denim, the boots can ground a shorter hemline, and the skirt can be dressed down with a simple knit. It’s a reminder that a statement piece doesn’t need an entirely new wardrobe built around it.

Industry observers note that for Gray, the best outfits leave room for a little experimentation. “I love an unexpected pairing,” she claims. “That’s why I love the dress and the bomber!” It’s a simple philosophy, one that gets to the heart of personal style. It’s about recognizing what you like, finding interesting ways to put things together, and having the confidence to wear them your way. H&M Studio Holiday 2026 offers plenty of starting points, from dramatic silhouettes to tactile accessories and everyday staples with a twist. What happens next is up to you.

Tech Report: Are You a Super Ager? This Competition Will Be the Judge of That

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart.
  • It has been revealed that as soon as the volunteer says “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over.
  • The challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alan Krepack stands with his hands on his hips and takes a deep breath as he sizes up the Over Under: an obstacle with a high wooden box and low wooden beam spread 10 meters apart. Music booms over the speakers and other competitors shuffle around the cavernous room of the Armory Track in Washington Heights, New York, but Krepack stays laser-focused, thanks to years of meditation practice.

It has been revealed that as soon as the volunteer says “go” he sprints to the box, plants his hands, and hoists his feet up and over. As he lands on the other side, he sprints to the beam, dropping down into an army crawl. “Take your time, take your time,” his son yells from the sidelines. Krepack reaches the far end, rushes back, and repeats the sequence again before crossing the line in 51 seconds. To cool down, he paces back and forth with his hands on his head. “I think I’m a sprinter, I’m a jumper, but then it’s like, fuck, no, I’m 73 years old,” he says, catching his breath.

The challenge is just the first of eight trials Krepeck will tackle throughout the day alongside his sons, Harrison and Aaron, at the Super Age Games, a fitness and mental competition designed to assess abilities associated with healthy aging. On November 7th, the inaugural day-long event drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries, and about 70% of participants were between the ages of 40 and 64. Krepeck agreed to let me shadow him to understand this newly introduced event through the lens of someone who is, in fact, aging, and would like to do so gracefully.

The name of the Games comes from a buzzword that originated in the longevity world: super ager. The term was originally coined by Northwestern University researchers to describe adults over 80 whose memories rival those of people 30 years younger. These days it’s thrown around on podcasts and in books to describe anyone who defies both the typical trajectory of both cognitive and physical aging.

The inaugural Super Age Games drew 530 athletes from 42 states and 15 countries.

From crawling across a cargo net to reading microexpressions, the challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill. At the end, athletes see where they rank among their age group and receive their “Super Age,” learning how their body’s physical fitness stacks up against the general U.S. population’s.

Recent findings suggest that in an era where your average middle-aged midwestern dad is training for Hyrox, and a new, outlandishly extreme challenge is being invented every few months, the Super Age games are a low-key counterpoint to raw, stunty, athleticism, born from the metric-obsessed fitness subcultures who prize longevity above all. And now that fitness trackers like Whoop or Apple Watch can track VO2max, heart rate variability, and resting heart rates, that group continues to grow. Along the way, these stats have become status symbols on par with owning a Lamborghini. And now that overall health is quantifiable, fitness values have become less about just how fast you run or how much you lift, but how slowly aging.

Industry observers note that it follows that, despite its name, Super Age Games isn’t just for aging athletes. The crowd there leaned middle-aged, and the youngest person at the competition was 21. As we stood by the dead hang station, Krepak pointed across the room at a brolic young man who looked like he could be an NFL prospect: “That dude’s a serious athlete,” he notes, as we watched him run around the track cradling a sandbag on his shoulder.

Unlike competitions like Hyrox, where athletes race through a sequence of workouts against the clock, the Super Age Games allows competitors to rest as long as they need between trials. In fact, Junior Kennedy, the fitness program director for the Games, encourages it. “There's no rush,” he indicates. “The goal is to get through each event as intentionally as you can. We need to understand what it means to recover.”.

Industry observers note that each trial was developed with a certain longevity marker in mind, and developed with input from researchers at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, a leading nonprofit research center based in Novato, California dedicated to understanding aging. The Over Under, for example, tests agility by judging how fast you can change levels and switch directions. Meanwhile, the Synapse, a challenge where participants track moving balls on a screen and identify them after they've been shuffled around, is meant to measure cognitive processing.

Challenges in the competition measure longevity markers like functional strength, aerobic capacity, balance, and cognitive skill.

According to recent reports, krepack, a psychologist and lifelong athlete from Mill Valley, California, first heard about the event through its founder, David Stewart. Stewart is a media founder behind two niche longevity platforms, AGEIST and Super Age, where he writes about longevity, wellness, and redefining aging (one of his website testimonial’s says he has made aging “cool and aspirational.”). Krepack’s generally a skeptic of the profit-driven modern wellness industry—“I've always had a jaded view of all of that stuff,” he says—but he has followed both Stewart and the Buck Institutes’ work for years.

The competition appealed to Krepack, in part because he’s spent decades cultivating a consistent exercise routine he’s proud of. He played baseball in college and has spent much of his life skiing, cycling, and playing other sports. These days, his schedule revolves around a handful of rituals: bike rides on Mondays and Fridays, a Saturday hike with a friend, gardening, yoga, and Zen meditation most days. When he signed up for the Games in June, he altered his exercise routine, lifted more weights, practiced hanging from a bar, and experimented with the Neurotracker cognitive test online.

Yet all that training didn’t prepare Krepack for the biggest surprise of his day. After scoring well on both the Inferno (the assault bike VO2max test) and Synapse, next came the fourth trial: the “Tightrope,” a balance challenge that requires competitors to walk along a low beam while carrying a water-filled bag, taking as many consecutive steps as they can in two minutes without falling. He had expected to excel, thanks to years of skiing and yoga. Instead, he struggled to keep steady as the water shifted inside the bag. As his foot slipped off the bar, his eyes got wide. “I can’t believe my balance,” he notes. “That’s my one disappointment in life now.”.

Alan Krepack's sons Harrison and Aaron during the “tightrope” challenge.

It has been revealed that krepack was still hard on himself as we walked over to the dead hang trial. But after beating both his sons’ times, he seemed to get his competitive spirit back. He pushed through the remaining challenge determined to finish strong. And he did: By the end of the Games, he had placed second overall, with scores adjusted for age.

A few days after the competition, I checked in with Krepack to ask him how he’d processed the event. He responded with screenshots of his scores. His highest score came from the cargo net, which he credited to sheer determination rather than any particular finesse: “due to my will and overcoming an unconventional and desperate style!” he texted me, “Plus my sons were great support and focus partners.”.

But the Games were also a reality check about aging: “I left there feeling both young and old,” he tells me on a phone call. As he watched his sons rocket through the obstacles, he was forced to confront how much of his athleticism he’d lost. “They just flew over it. They were so fluid, and so fast,” he indicates. “I’m not 30 or 40 or 50 or 60 anymore.”.

Despite all the longevity industry's promises of maintaining youth, Krepack sees little value in denying the inevitable. Aging well, he indicates, is about “accepting, improving, and doing your best. It’s not a denial of who you are at this point in life.” The goal, he says, is to make the most of what you’re still capable of.

The Hunger Games franchise, including The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, is currently streaming on Hulu, Disney+, Tubi, and Peacock. So your guess is as good as mine. All of the above? A secret, fifth place? Who can say??

So that’s a six-month waiting period. That would mean that Sunrise on the Reaping will likely be streaming by May of next year, 2027. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Despite being sisters who both work in Hollywood, Dakota and Elle Fanning have starred opposite each other just once.
  • Twenty-five years later, Elle and Dakota are sharing the screen for the second time ever in the film adaptation of The Nightingale, a war story about two sisters who take separate paths during a trying time in France’s history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Despite being sisters who both work in Hollywood, Dakota and Elle Fanning have starred opposite each other just once. The movie, titled I Am Sam, was released in 2001 and featured the girls when they were 6 and 2 years old. That remained their only joint acting credit—until now.

Twenty-five years later, Elle and Dakota are sharing the screen for the second time ever in the film adaptation of The Nightingale, a war story about two sisters who take separate paths during a trying time in France’s history. Here’s everything we know about the film so far.

The Nightingale is adapted from Kristin Hannah’s 2015 novel of the same name. The summary for the book reads: “The Nightingale tells the stories of two sisters, separated by years and experience, by ideals, passion, and circumstance, each embarking on her own dangerous path toward survival, love, and freedom in German-occupied, war-torn France—a heartbreakingly beautiful novel that celebrates the resilience of the human spirit and the durability of women.”.

It has been revealed that elle and Dakota will star as Isabelle Rossignol and Vianne Mauriac, respectively. The cast also includes Douglas Hodge, Edmund Donovan, Mark Rylance as Julien Rossignol, Albrecht Schuch, Gwilym Lee, Shira Haas as Rachel de Champlain, and Vinette Robinson.

In the sisters’ joint interview with ELLE earlier this year, the pair admitted that they were nervous about acting together on-screen for The Nightingale, but “the power of the book” drew them in.

Industry observers note that “There are lots of complicated things within the story, but at its core, it’s actually a quite simple story, which is the everlasting love between these two sisters, set within a time period that is so rife with tragedy,” Dakota explained. “It’s clearly a story that people are able to put themselves in, in some capacity, and feel all those emotions and the dynamic between our characters. So that was just impossible to ignore.”.

Dakota continued, “It’s the first time that it felt like an undeniable thing. Whereas when we were younger, it felt a little more clichéd and it didn’t feel emotionally right.”.

It has been revealed that elle noted that coming together on a project feels fitting now because they’ve had time to grow as separate individuals. “At the age we are now, after having forged our own paths and our careers and acting styles separately, being able to come together just feels right. And we have to do it so people will stop asking us,” she noted. Dakota added, “We’re like, ‘We’re going to literally disappoint everyone we’ve ever met if we don’t make this happen somehow.’”.

The trailer for the movie arrived on November 19. In the footage, the sisters share a moment of tenderness, lying in bed together and smiling at each other, but Vianne (Dakota) rapidly reminds her sister Isabelle (Elle) that she needs to keep herself out of harm’s way.

“I have one job: to keep my family safe. And you’re part of my family whether you like it or not,” Vianne tells her sister. Isabelle, however, has a different attitude. “They’re at our doorstep. In our homes,” she retorts. “We must show them that we will fight back.” Isabelle ultimately uses her rage to join the rebellion, putting herself and her family at risk.

Watch the trailer in full below.

The Nightingale opens in theaters on March 19, 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, yesterday, Hailey Bieber took her obsession with ’90s minimalism one step further with a reference to the ultimate ‘90s minimalist: Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy.
  • A few weeks ago, savvy shoppers spotted the look for sale on the RealReal.
  • It sat on the site long enough to make the Instagram rounds, but someone snatched it up before the site had time to mark it down.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, yesterday, Hailey Bieber took her obsession with ’90s minimalism one step further with a reference to the ultimate ‘90s minimalist: Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy. For a talk at the 2026 DealBook Summit here in New York, she and her stylist Dani Michelle pulled a Yohji Yamamoto look from Spring 1998, the one with a black, high-necked jacket with a line of delicate buttons paired with a white linen column skirt so famously worn by CBK in June 1998. It did what it was supposed to do: Stop us in our scrolling. But it jogged something else in the collective consciousness of fashion lovers everywhere. Hadn’t this jacket just made the rounds on our feeds?

A few weeks ago, savvy shoppers spotted the look for sale on the RealReal. Bessette-Kennedy’s reverence for Yohji Yamamoto is one that fashion’s acolytes tend to share, so it didn’t take long for the listing to go viral. The description identified its starry provenance: “From the Spring/Summer 1998 Collection; as worn by Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy in 1998 and worn by Winona Ryder for the season 5 premiere of 'Stranger Things' in 2025.”.

TRR listed the jacket for $7,025. It sat on the site long enough to make the Instagram rounds, but someone snatched it up before the site had time to mark it down. The jacket sold for full price on November 6, less than two weeks before the DealBook Summit.

According to recent reports, could it be that Bieber scrolls for vintage Yohji on the RealReal like the rest of us? Does she have saved searches? Is she watching her obsessions with the eyes of a hawk? (Or has she outsourced this job to Michelle or someone on her team?) Bazaar reached out to the RealReal, and a spokesperson revealed that while all customer data is private, they know that Bieber’s look did not come from them. Well, it was fun to imagine. But just the possibility that this could have happened is enough to make you think.

Michelle’s post of the look does not reveal her source, though days later, she confirmed the source to be Tab Vintage. The vintage resale platform Shy mentioned in comment sections that it recently sold the same piece. Another one of the jackets, also without a proven link to CBK’s personal wardrobe, sold via the Fashion Auctioneer in March for $12,500. That’s the thing with ready-to-wear: It’s not one-of-a-kind. Bessette-Kennedy bought her jacket off the rack, which means there are multiple versions floating around out there.

Industry observers note that if you scroll down the jacket’s sold page on the RealReal to the “Related Items” section, you’ll find multiple listings of the Cruise 2005 Chanel jacket Andy Sachs famously wore in The Devil Wears Prada, priced at roughly ten grand. “Similar style seen on Anne Hathaway in 'The Devil Wears Prada,'” the description reads. “We are seeing more and more archival pieces with incredible cultural provenance come in on consignment,” states Kristen Naiman, chief brand officer at the RealReal. “And we love helping these shards of fashion history resurface in pop culture.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s become common practice for major stylists to mine specialty vintage stores for these megawatt, nostalgia-driven red carpet references. Just look at Law Roach’s Instagram account, where he documents pulling 1950s Balenciaga for Kim Kardashian from Lily et Cie, a source that specializes in museum-quality vintage. But as this thought experiment exemplifies, these transactions are becoming more normalized.

Naiman continues: “Whether you know Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy or not, there is now an entire newly introduced generation coveting this Yohji Yamamoto look on Hailey Bieber, and it has a renewed desirability because of that. And that’s the fun of being a fashion hobbyist and TRR enthusiast. You not only love the piece, you know the love story behind the piece. It’s a way to participate in fashion history. You can spend years coveting a jacket that has left an indelible mark on culture and then, one day, find it in your size.”.

Sources indicate that which brings us back to that Yohji jacket that sold on November 6. We know Bieber wasn’t the one who purchased it, but some lucky person did, and now they own a piece of fashion history. Wonder how many other people have the same one.

Aside from the look being a clear classic in the world of jewelry (horseshoes were popular in Victorian-era jewels), today’s examples vary from sparkly creations to more minimal, toned-down pieces with everyday appeal. No matter the aesthetic, the jewelry of the Year of the Fire Horse is strong: This era only comes around every 60 years in the Chinese zodiac and is stated to represent strength, independence, and fearlessness.

Recent findings suggest that celebrities are clearly fans: Taylor Swift just wore two double-layered horseshoe pendants to announce her Grammy nomination. Horse-ified jewelry also spanned the runway. For spring/summer 2027, both Gucci and Celine revisited the archival horsebit hardware detail and reworked it in a contemporary way to highlight the beautiful lines and sculptural symmetry of the timeless motif. Elsewhere, Chloé’s statement belt covered in huge running horses has been a fashion girl favorite and is the equivalent of jewelry for your waist.

There is perhaps nothing more classic than a chunky horseshoe ring or a horse-themed charm. Verragio and Oscar Heyman each reworked the symbol in gemstone-studded bracelets and double-motif rings. Elsewhere, Lionheart makes a slew of gloriously stunning oversize horse-head pendants and brooches brimming with diamonds and, sometimes, accessorized with mother-of-pearl saddles. The brand also partners directly with 13 Hands Equine Rescue, a nonprofit sanctuary located in Clinton Corners, New York.

Sources indicate that but this year, equestrian jewelry is not horsing around when it comes to experimenting. One such example is Hermès’s latest collection, which has an obvious horse connection: saddles, diamond-decked horse heads, and golden saddles. Titled “Into the Horsescape,” the 90-piece lineup is quite literally the horse girl’s dream: lassos in the form of massive baguette-cut diamonds and glimmering oversize horsebit bracelets replete with pavé brown and white diamonds. Pomellato also showcased a carved horse cameo surrounded by brown diamonds and suspended from a delicate rose-gold Dressage-link chain.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to lean into your inner horse girl in a more subtle, everyday way, Gucci’s iconic horsebit rings, refined drop earrings, and sleek bangles offer a sophisticated and versatile place to start your collection. Going vintage is another option: Equestrian themes have been reinterpreted in the jewelry space for hundreds of years now, so there’s ample opportunity. One thing is clear: Horse girl jewelry is galloping from the archives to the runway and into everyday style.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Blade Runner franchise imagines a bleak dystopian future, one where the world has been ravaged by nuclear war and humans are burdened with inequality and threatened by rogue robots. But if everyone dressed like Hunter Schafer, how bad could it really be?

While promoting her upcoming miniseries, Blade Runner 2099—which serves as a sequel to the Blade Runner (1982) and Blade Runner 2049 (2017) movies—Schafer has been on a hot streak of futuristic, otherworldly looks.

So far, she’s worn everything from a neon-green Nihl hoodie covered in beaded florals to a double-layer Lii minidress that appeared to peel open from the back. Now, her latest ensemble plays with time in a different way—by looking space-age, sure, but also by uniting decades of fashion history.

At the Blade Runner 2099 photocall in London earlier today, Schafer stepped out in a pop-art inspired look that combined periods of Prada fashion.

According to recent reports, styled by Dara, Schafer embraced the exposed-underwear trend with a satin, cerulean bra, which was paired with a white wrap-around midi skirt with a patch of neon-green color. Both were pulled directly from the Prada Spring/Summer 2027 ready-to-wear collection by Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons.

While Schafer has long been a supporter of the storied Italian brand, here, she and Dara pulled out a reference for the true fans, layering on a transparent, PVC raincoat pulled from Prada’s Fall 2002 collection.

With its thick black trim, the vinyl outerwear could have been plucked straight from the pages of a comic book. And to match the edges, the coat was cinched with an inky leather belt, while Schafer wore a pair of pointy black heels down low. For a finishing touch, she rocked electric-blue eyeshadow that winked to the color of her bra.

Sometimes, it can be hard to feel optimistic about the future. But at least Schafer is here to imagine one that’s wonderfully colorful, fun, and stylish.

Industry News: The Scoop with Moynat’s Aydha Mehnaz: On Launching Her Fresh Consultancy Venture Avari

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week.
  • Industry observers note that this week’s guest is Aydha Mehnaz, whose day job is head of global brand relations at Moynat, purveyor of trunks and the monogrammed totes your fashionable colleague started carrying around in the last couple of years.
  • Aydha with Paris Hilton at Mugler SS24 where Paris made her Paris runway debut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week. This will be a way for the Vogue Business community to synthesize and reflect on the latest headlines and get a little inside scoop every Friday.

Industry observers note that this week’s guest is Aydha Mehnaz, whose day job is head of global brand relations at Moynat, purveyor of trunks and the monogrammed totes your fashionable colleague started carrying around in the last couple of years. I met Aydha when she worked in the PR department at Mugler, alongside Bertrand Le Gall (now the image director at Moynat), while I was at Selfridges. I remember it was the 30th anniversary of the brand’s Angel perfume that we were working on.

Aydha with Paris Hilton at Mugler SS24 where Paris made her Paris runway debut.

In a recent development, we hit it off because Aydha is cool and ambitious in all the right ways. She grew up in Bangladesh and studied biochemistry before leaving it all behind about 10 years ago for a Masters at ESMOD in Paris. From there, she landed at Mugler but, in between all that, she also started one of the first and best Tumblrs on modest fashion, called Minazification. The blog doesn’t work anymore, but Aydha very much does. She’s recently started a newly introduced venture, which is what we are talking about today.

Sources indicate that I recently debuted Avari, my communications consultancy for brands and talent who want to reach the Southeastern consumer or Southeastern brands who want to do the opposite. I built it with my brother, who is based in Dhaka, because it was key for us to operate in four different time zones.

I come from Bangladesh but moved to Paris about 10 years ago, and now I am in Fresh York. Throughout my career, while moving through those luxury spaces, I’ve been very conscious of how those places shape me, and Avari has the same geographical footprint as I do. The word in Sanskrit speaks to something that’s obscure, almost like a shapeshifter. Luxury no longer holds the same values it once did because the consumer has changed and has a more multicultural, constantly changing attitude.

Aydha with Jordan Clarkson of the NY Knicks during the Moynat Kasing Lung shoot.

We want to be a partner for brands and talents, making sure you can become whoever you want. For me, the main objective is to nurture talent from South Asia. There isn’t enough representation in Western media, and for those who are there, there isn’t enough guidance on how to package themselves to enter the Western market. There is so much talent coming from that part of the world, and particularly from Bangladesh since the July Uprising of 2024, but few know where to look or how. I do.

Talk to me about the difference between the Bangladesh you left as a student and the Bangladesh you are building a business for 10 years later.

In a recent development, when I left, the creative pool was quite small. There weren’t many people doing latest things; it was more iterations of what you would see from India or from Pakistan. Now there are so many designers, chefs, photographers, and all sorts of other artists who see themselves as global talents rather than being limited by their surroundings. This is why, for Avari, it was so key to set up a hub in Dhaka.

Aydha with guests attending at Moynat’s Travelling Popup in Chicago.

You are the first Bangladeshi on the Scoop, so I have to ask you about the factory protests. What can you tell us about what is really happening on the ground?

This is my very own observation, and I am not speaking for anyone, but protests are not newly introduced in Bangladesh or anywhere. Protests happen in Paris too, right? And the truth is always somewhere in the middle. In Bangladesh, you have a set of factories that are not regulated. They probably treat their workers very poorly and keep costs low by avoiding taking safety measures. But then you also have factories that are actually charging you a premium price, giving you the polo or the Carhartt sweatshirt you wear every day. This sweater I am wearing is actually made in Bangladesh.

So those factories are providing healthcare and safe facilities for their employees. The people who don’t get the right treatment are obviously going to protest. But the thing is that whenever these conversations take place in Western media, only one side, the bad side of Bangladesh, is shown. And there are also local people who profit from exacerbating that picture.

Does Bangladesh care about James Bond?

Of course, the memes are crazy. I like the one about Robert Pattinson getting all the jobs.

In a recent development, it’s interesting how much things have changed in 10-20 years. When I was growing up in Greece, global news didn’t have the same effect, whereas now we all see the same memes at the same time, everywhere. But we are all still culturally different.

Industry observers note that right, and that has affected how global consumers behave. As an example, Bangkok for the Bangladeshi is considered a second Dhaka — you literally walk on the street and run into people you know. Because the high earners from South Asia go to shop in Thailand, but also in India, the UAE, America, and Europe. South Asians have so many cultural similarities, and we often speak each other’s language too.

It has been revealed that my introduction to luxury wasn’t the Western brands but my mum’s heirloom jewelry that she is waiting for me to inherit. We are talking about 24-karat pieces that have been passed down from generation to generation. You can see how a brand like Sabyasachi brings that into the modern world, and there are so many other local creatives with a global view. Locals are finally investing in South Asian culture and South Asian art. With Avari, the idea is: how do we fit into that?

According to recent reports, applications for the 2027 LVMH prize are now open. Who would you like to see apply?

Khanums, a British label with Bangladeshi roots, and Menka from Bangladesh, who make these handwoven sarees with heirloom weavers. Also, Kartik Research from India is fab, but he’s already taken part.

#31682. Latest Update: Wig Business Is Substantial Business

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1559 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Wig Business Is Substantial Business

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the hair category is presently a hotbed for growth.
  • After 40 years in hairdressing, hairstylist and salon owner Charlotte Mensah has seen trends come and go, but notes that extensions have had enduring appeal.
  • In a recent development, “Full hair has always been in style,” says Charlotte Mensah.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the hair category is presently a hotbed for growth. Alongside much innovation in existing products, the past decade has seen hair transplants, scalp serums, and novel treatment concepts like head spas surge in popularity. And the category holds appeal across many demographics, from the more traditional mid-life market to burgeoning legions of ‘looksmaxxers’ and ever younger consumers seeking interventions for early-stage thinning, pattern baldness and GLP1-induced hair loss. While many consumers are investing in supplements, serums or aesthetic treatments to address the issue, another cohort is spending big on extensions and wigs.

After 40 years in hairdressing, hairstylist and salon owner Charlotte Mensah has seen trends come and go, but notes that extensions have had enduring appeal. “Even with my clients that embrace their natural look, many are seeing value in adding volume/length and will request a weft that matches their hair texture to achieve this,” she explains. What’s more, extensions and wigs have become less of a secret, considered desirable across race, gender and other consumer groups. “The appearance of full, healthy hair is always fashionable. These days, we have newly introduced methods like tapes and synthetic fibers that can simulate human hair, making hair extensions more accessible to everyone,” she adds.

In a recent development, “Full hair has always been in style,” says Charlotte Mensah. “I’ve noticed clients are increasingly interested in extensions that mirror their hair’s natural texture.”.

As revenues go, the wig business is a lucrative business. The SKUs in this sector — wigs, wefts and other hair extension systems, such as lace toupees and semi-permanent, bonded K-tips — commonly necessitate multibuy purchases to achieve desired hairstyles and individually command price tags upwards of £250.

At the top end of the market, a single wig or set of extensions can sell for tens of thousands, with long extension lengths, made-to-measure customizations and laborious finishes justifying costs. Value perception is high, thanks to human hair’s product lifespan, reusability and styling versatility. Together with growing hair loss concerns, these factors encourage consumers to adopt an investment-purchase mindset that makes for higher average order values in the extensions space.

In a recent development, having earned £20,000 through 30 orders in just 10 minutes on launch day, CEO Denise Nwogbu has honed a strategy for success here. Her wig brand Go Glueless positions its product offer as a “hair appointment in a box”, eliminating the friction associated with installing specialist extensions. Customers are drawn to the convenience and seamless nature of the wigs, which do not require adhesives to style — instead, they can be secured through elastic headbands on the wig’s interior that keep it fitted in place on the user’s scalp. She notes this ease of installation has driven high waitlist demand and often results in sellouts across the range on drop days.

Denise Nwogbu, CEO and founder of Go Glueless, has found success positioning her product as a “salon appointment in a box.”.

Industry observers note that “We limit releases to four times a year and use a pre-order model. This allows time to carefully source single-donor, virgin hair, then handcraft and customize each bespoke unit,” Nwogbu shares. “Provenance is everything — I chose my supplier in Vietnam because she has a real relationship with each woman who grows and sells their hair for the production of the extensions. She does not delegate to hair collectors, she goes personally to the villages to find willing volunteers that have not been coerced into cutting their hair. She can tell you their exact age, name and lifestyle, and pays them fairly with an understanding of virgin hair value in the West.”.

Sources indicate that by the time the hair reaches Go Glueless headquarters in Birmingham, it has been cuticle-tested to ensure quality and longevity. Then, a team of wig specialists construct, color and cut units to exact customer measurements. Attracting an affluent, often time-poor clientele of professional women and public figures, Go Glueless’s USP lies in doing the labor so the end consumer has it completely removed.

On launch day, Go Glueless made £20,000 in online preorders. Now, the brand has opened its first IRL space —a suite where customers can browse and get bespoke fittings for their wigs.

“It’s a salon experience with no skills needed, but education is also vital: every customer gets access to exclusive tutorials through GG Academy, our online portal,” Denise notes. This in itself is a clever strategy, attracting large audiences already searching for terms like “wig install tutorial”, which has amassed 478,000 impressions on TikTok. “And we educate our clients about help available to them if they are buying wigs to manage medical hair loss — many with conditions like alopecia or cancer aren’t aware of their entitlement to VAT relief.”.

In the wig business, hair loss sufferers are likely to be engaged, repeat customers, presenting major sales opportunities. But profits aren’t the only piece of the puzzle — the most impactful brands focus on corporate social responsibility, too.

Market leader Beauty Works, whose assortment includes both professional-grade extensions and DIY clip-ins, is a case in point. Its relationship with the charity Little Lady Locks, which provides free medical wigs and hair services to minors with medical hair loss, is symbiotic: the charity benefits from Beauty Works’s financial investment, resources and expert volunteers, while Beauty Works can exhibit purpose-driven values, benefiting from enhanced brand image and positive engagement within aligned communities.

Beauty Works donates hair extensions to Little Lady Locks, helping the charity provide free wigs to boost the confidence of hair loss sufferers under 18.

Elsewhere, the brand is significant on avoiding ethical quandaries common to the hair trade by enforcing strict compliance throughout its supply chain. “Our human hair is voluntarily sold by individuals who are fairly compensated,” says Randilyn Dela Cruz, product architect and vice president of development at Beauty Works’ parent tech giant BIG. “Our sourcing standards require a respectful process and prohibit child labor, forced labor and sourcing from regions where there are known human-rights violations,” she details.

Industry observers note that sourcing is an crucial aspect for any wig business to get right, especially given a black market of sorts exists. A far cry from the luxury products they’re promoted as in the West, some vendors acquire hair of dubious origin, obscure its imperfections and sell to unwitting customers overseas at a high markup. An ITV News exposé found this can include waste hair pulled from sewer drains in India, as well as “floor hair” collected from the ground of salons by cheap laborers desperate to cash in on the lucrative trade.

It has been revealed that “It’s ‘the fast fashion’ side of wigs,” Denise stresses, going on to explain that these vendors chemically relax the waste balls of hair — which are made up of several cut hairs with different properties because they are from multiple donors’ heads — to the point where it appears flawless. “They often then market it deceptively under names like ‘bone straight’. “You couldn’t tell with the naked eye, but when you use that kind of hair to produce hair extensions, time always tells. It frizzes up, tangles easily and is unpredictable after the chemical coatings wash off, and business owners risk having that happen in the hands of your consumer if you don’t do your due diligence at the point of sourcing,” she warns.

It has been revealed that hence, Denise insists on flying to Vietnam personally to inspect and test the quality of any hair used in the making of Go Glueless units. It’s expensive work, but something she recommends as worthwhile for upcoming businesses hoping to break into the luxury wig space.

Recent findings suggest that another common source of hair that can pose ethical dilemmas is Indian temple hair. This hair comes from Hindu tonsuring ceremonies, in which some donors shave their heads under the religious belief that it releases past spiritual baggage. Others agree to shed their hair as a sacred sacrifice to be devoted to specific deities. These individuals are often left in the dark about the final destination of their hair and its huge monetary value if it is later sold on to wig companies at auction, and they often receive no part of the profits, according to a recent report from the BBC. Questions around exploitation in these cases can influence perception among discerning end consumers, and are worth investigating to reduce brand risk.

Model wears Synths 2: an extension that uses collagen-based fibers to add length and volume without the need for human hair or more toxic synthetic alternatives.

To sidestep sourcing issues entirely, Charlotte Mensah often opts for “man-made fibers that have been designed to perform like human hair and that can still be styled with heat tools” in her salon. This is an area of category expansion, with synthetic products from Outré reaching viral fame and plant-based hair brands like Rebundle, Knott and Ruka Hair attracting new audiences with innovative alternatives to traditional human hair extensions.

Ruka Hair’s latest invention (a plastic-free, collagen-based braiding fiber called Synths 2) became the first-ever hair extension of its kind to land in Sephora doors this summer. Stockist support of this caliber affirms it: the wig business is big business indeed, and with the right sourcing, can set savvy founders up for exponential growth.

“It Was Never About Fashion”: Emily in Paris’s Costume Designer Reveals the Method to Her Madness

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emily in Paris premiered when audiences needed it most.
  • The love for Emily in Paris was anything but unanimous.
  • Industry observers note that for six seasons, Fitoussi curated a wardrobe fit for Emily, a bright-eyed young woman unafraid to try something fresh, to break the rules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emily in Paris premiered when audiences needed it most. The Netflix original, created by Sex and the City producer Darren Star, offered an escapist fantasy: a young girl trying to find love and success in Paris in October 2020. The show functioned as a reprieve from the pandemic, a dreamy alternative in which we could vicariously live through Emily (Lily Collins) as she gallivanted around the City of Light. It was and still is delectably digestible television.

The love for Emily in Paris was anything but unanimous. Critics wasted no time tearing the show apart, with some targeting its depictions of French culture or claiming the script lacked the bite of Star’s previous television highlights. The criticism extended to Emily’s idiosyncratic wardrobe, with some writing that the clothing leaned hard on American stereotypes of French fashion or looked cartoonish, with clashing patterns and bright colors. Costume designer Marylin Fitoussi took these criticisms head-on and doubled down. Emily’s outfits weren’t meant to be couture or designer; they were meant to dress a girl finding her sense of self, expressing her desire to explore the unknown.

Industry observers note that for six seasons, Fitoussi curated a wardrobe fit for Emily, a bright-eyed young woman unafraid to try something fresh, to break the rules. This mirrors Fitoussi’s personal philosophy on clothing: that fashion is meant to break rules, to push boundaries, to provide a space of unrelenting experimentation. Ahead of the sixth season, SCAD FASH Museum of Fashion + Film compiles six seasons’ worth of outfits in “Emily in Paris: Fashion Without Rules,” on view through March 14, 2027. The exhibition lives up to its name; for the designer, clothing is a mode of expression that lets anyone feel free, wherever they are. It offers a character study, tracing Emily’s evolution from a doe-eyed expat to a well-versed Parisian resident. (And worry not, there are also looks from Emily’s chic boss Sylvie—played with devastating elegance by Philippine Leroy-Beaulieu.).

Ahead of season 6, Bazaar sat down with Fitoussi at SCAD Fashion in Atlanta to discuss working with Lily Collins, her swan song for Emily in Paris, and how everyone has the potential for creativity.

Marylin Fitoussi: I don’t recall a contemporary TV show being in the spotlight in this way. Generally, when you think of an exhibition, you think of period pieces or couture pieces. The show is really part of pop culture now!

Sources indicate that MF: I was surprised when fashion magazines [criticized the show] at the beginning. I’m not a fashion designer, [but] I love fashion and I love clothes. This show was not about fashion at the beginning. [Emily] is a bubbly character with a very strong personality from Chicago; she couldn’t have come dressed in Comme des Garçons or in Yamamoto. I needed to have this cultural shock. She’s a fish-out-of-water character, and we needed something to catch the audience’s eyes. When you want to show people that you love the culture but you can’t express it because you don’t know the codes, you don’t speak the language, the only way you find it is through clothes. It was never about “fashion.” Sometimes, it’s about creativity, individuality, making something not trendy at all. The audience got that, and fashion magazines didn’t get it, so they killed me.

Recent findings suggest that MF: Many times, I’ve asked myself, “Why does this little gingham suit have so much influence?” It’s quite simple. It was the most duplicated, copied, reposted, fan-arted, and used as a Halloween costume. It touched people because it was for them. The French can have their own version of it, their own concept, but for the entire world, it was this one little girly, timeless outfit with the red beret, the red lips, the red soul.

In a recent development, MF: She read the bad press after the release of season 1, and we had a talk. I mentioned they hated it in France; they find it hideous. [I asked her] “Do you want me to change [it]?” She was smiling and said, “No, we can’t, and we won’t please everybody. We need to keep this strong DNA. We need to continue to have this unexpected silhouette because it’s what catches the audience’s eye.” It’s a guilty pleasure. We can say, I love it.

Recent findings suggest that it opens a way for the audience to see fashion in a different way, where you can mix in an awkward way and free people from this law where you shouldn’t [do that]. Coco Chanel used to say, “Before leaving a room, look at yourself in the mirror and take something out.” I always say, “Put something more on.”.

MF: I wanted to present a more elevated version, more mature, more evolved, but still true to what she was and what she is, with an eclectic combination and a little bit awkward. She knows the French rules, but as I do, she finds French fashion so boring. In general, I find that fashion is less and less interesting. Why are fashion and celebrity stylists sourcing more and more from archives? What it’s showing is that now everything is the same. Everything is boring, and I understand why. They need to sell the show! We don’t have to sell anything. We have to sell dreams, illusions, craziness, boldness. People watch the show in groups. Some people say, “I love it,” and some say, “I hate it,” and they have a dialogue and fight and have a good [time]. We love that.

Recent findings suggest that MF: A young designer wants to be famous right away. Fame doesn’t happen, and it doesn’t matter. You need to be happy with what you’re doing. With costume design versus fashion design, you can be much freer. You don’t have anything to sell, and you don’t have to design the “It bag.” If your show is successful, it’s a win-win for everybody. To see that, you need to be true to your vision. You need to be true to your gut feeling, to your vision, to your DNA. Talent is not enough; you need to be at the right place at the right time. Being discovered by Darren Star … he changed my life. At some point, you find the right project for you.

You need to work a lot to take care of every detail. You need to be strong and push the boundaries. You need to try to show a different way to see costumes and clothes, to see that everything is possible…. Style begins when fear ends. You don’t want to please everybody, and I’m always attracted to people who dress in a different way, and I’m never judgmental. To create something is to expose yourself. It’s very vulnerable. It’s brave.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

📖 Baca

Tech Report: From Practical Gifts to Wellness Moments: Holiday Trends to Watch for 2026

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as the holidays beckon, a younger, fashion-led contingent of consumers across the US and Europe are upping their spend despite inflation, higher living costs and economic volatility.
  • Recent findings suggest that “[US consumers] are signaling that they’re going to continue to be resilient shoppers and lean into the holiday season,” states Brian McCarthy, Deloitte’s retail strategy leader, pinpointing millennials as the top spenders this year by a long shot — in part because of life stage.
  • Across the board, high-net-worth individuals (HNWI) are more discerning than ever — spending more where necessary, for gifts centered on individuality, performance, wellness and sentimentality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as the holidays beckon, a younger, fashion-led contingent of consumers across the US and Europe are upping their spend despite inflation, higher living costs and economic volatility. The situation doesn’t make sense on paper, but on department store floors, the verdict is clear: The holidays are still big business for luxury — they just look a little different.

Recent findings suggest that “[US consumers] are signaling that they’re going to continue to be resilient shoppers and lean into the holiday season,” states Brian McCarthy, Deloitte’s retail strategy leader, pinpointing millennials as the top spenders this year by a long shot — in part because of life stage. “Millennials and Gen Z now have some discretionary spending, and they’re starting to hit the age where they have children,” he adds, advising that department stores focus on these two cohorts.

Across the board, high-net-worth individuals (HNWI) are more discerning than ever — spending more where necessary, for gifts centered on individuality, performance, wellness and sentimentality.

Industry observers note that deloitte’s holiday report predicts that average household holiday spending in the US will increase 4% year-on-year to $1,654 per household in 2026. In Europe, shoppers are expected to spend 3.4% more year-on-year this holiday season, per data from Mastercard. In the US, millennials and Gen Z will make up 50% of spending — a first since the annual study began — with both groups upping their spend at a double-digit rate year-on-year. Most holiday shoppers expect to spend the most money at either mass merchants or online, followed by department stores.

It has been revealed that mcCarthy highlights some core stats luxury retailers must consider: 72% of Gen Z say they’re interested in purchasing luxury goods as gifts for the holiday season, followed by 61% of millennials, 40% of Gen X, and 29% of baby boomers. The data also reveals that 76% of Gen Z initiative on gifting clothing and accessories, up from 67% last year.

The K-shaped economy — where the top end of the economy grows, but the lower end lags as inequalities widen — will ultimately benefit luxury fashion retailers, many of whom rely on the top percentile spenders to turn a profit. Nonetheless, even HNWIs are not immune to the same financial pressures as the aspirational and middle class, confirms Mintel. Analysts agree that price, value, convenience and product will dictate consumption across demographics this holiday period.

Holiday shopping at Harrods is well underway.

“Financial pressures continue to influence holiday spending, creating a resilient but resourceful consumer who is looking for deals and becoming more deliberate about where they spend,” says Brittany Steiger, Mintel’s associate principal for retail and e-commerce, noting that 72% of US luxury shoppers say price alone isn’t an indicator of luxury, and 41% consider discounts key.

According to recent reports, the macroeconomic environment is tricky, but it’s also a well-established mood of uncertainty. Per Mintel, 59% of shoppers admit financial stress is making it harder to celebrate in the way they prefer, but 39% are still willing to spend on truly meaningful purchases. Against this backdrop, the smartest retailers have risen to the challenge, aligning their product assortments with shifting consumer trends.

That said, the rollout of Christmas shopping remains largely the same. “We typically see two distinct phases: the first is about preparation, with clients investing in their own wardrobes ahead of festive celebrations,” says Simon Longland, Harrods’s director of fashion buying, pointing to partywear, evening-wear, knitwear and exceptional outerwear. Then, “as Christmas approaches, the focus shifts toward gifting.”.

Below, Vogue Business collates this year’s key gifting predictions.

For retailers, occasion dressing continues to drive growth over the holidays, but shoppers are displaying a more playful, casual approach, tracking with a younger consumer skew.

At Bloomingdale’s, ritzy festive occasionwear will be a key driver. “This holiday, we can put the pursuit of the perfect wardrobe on hold for a moment and indulge in the sheer joy of fashion for fashion’s sake,” indicates fashion director David Thielebeule. “After seasons of restraint, fashion is remembering how to have fun. Rich color, sumptuous textures and a little extravagance are making getting dressed feel exciting again.”.

Sebla Refiğ Devidas, Turkish retailer Communité’s chief merchandising officer, reports a similar appetite for eveningwear this holiday period. “In womenswear, we expect party dressing to be a major part of holiday shopping, especially pieces with interesting details that can be worn in different ways,” she notes. “There’s a sense of 1920s glamour in the lace, embellishments, fringed silk, and rich textures, reflected in pieces from Conner Ives, Dries Van Noten, Ann Demeulemeester, Simone Rocha, Anna October, Fforme and Enfants Riches Déprimés.”.

Sources indicate that at End, statement separates and directional designs from Simone Rocha, Cecilie Bahnsen, Rick Owens, Peachy Den and Gimaguas are outperforming traditional partywear. “We’re taking a broader and more fashion-led approach to occasion dressing this holiday season,” says Martin Wieczorek, End’s chief product officer. “We’re also seeing a notable shift toward separates over dresses, with customers seeking greater versatility and long-term wardrobe value, which is reflected in our assortment”.

Industry observers note that within menswear, Longland notes that while established party-wear brands and tailoring services will continue to play a significant role for Harrods this holiday season, the store is already seeing clients explore more pioneering attire. “We believe menswear today is as much about individual expression as it is about the traditional codes of dressing,” he says. “The festive season is a particularly interesting moment for this, whether clients are discovering a new designer or investing in beautifully tailored pieces for a special occasion.”.

Even among luxury shoppers, practicality is becoming a core tenet of holiday gifting.

“Confidence is low and spending is still up, which tells you people are not buying less, they are buying more carefully,” reports Christophe Roberts, founder and CCO of Upcoming York-based concept store Seed. What’s working? “Shoes, outerwear and the good $50 gift. The one big present is getting replaced by two or three smaller [practical] ones that actually say something about you.”.

Recent findings suggest that british retailer End reports an uptick in pragmatic premium outerwear gifting from brands including Our Legacy, Stone Island, Salomon, Arc’teryx, Barbour and Damson Madder. “We’re seeing menswear customers gravitate toward two key style directions,” notes Wieczorek, pointing to a continuation of outdoor dressing, functional accessories and hiking-influenced footwear. (In this vein, demand for Stone Island knits has grown 36% since October, per Lyst’s 2026 gift index.).

Recent findings suggest that on the other side of menswear gifting, End also reports a hunger for relaxed tailoring and elevated outerwear — “a long tailored coat is a must!” says Wieczorek — from brands such as Studio Nicholson, Auralee and YMC. In keeping with this desire for lasting purchases, Mintel reports that 71% of US men see luxury purchases as a personal milestone or marker of achievement, which makes meaningful wardrobe upgrades and keepsake gifts especially resonant. “We’re seeing strong momentum across jewellery and watches, a category that continues to gain traction during the gifting season as customers seek elevated, personal, enduring purchases,” says Wieczorek.

Calvin Klein underwear remains a strong stocking filler, boosted by the brand’s hit campaign.

In Fresh York-based concept store Essx, utility reigns supreme among menswear shoppers, bolstered by more experimental outerwear. “As the holiday season approaches, we expect to see a continued focus on utility shopping paired with experimental and statement outerwear. Leather has been one of our strongest categories over the past few seasons with VIPs and walk-in clients,” states Jackson Ray, store director. “We anticipate a continued desire for leather pants and jackets paired with sterling silver accessories and leather boots.”.

Recent findings suggest that essx also predicts keepsake pieces to perform. “Our customers always seek exclusive or limited items,” says Ray. “We have heavily invested in upscale accessories such as fine jewelry, eyewear, and footwear, which make for fantastic holiday gifts.

Recent findings suggest that unsurprisingly, underwear remains a trusty stocking filler for shoppers, especially this time round. Demand for men’s Calvin Klein underwear climbed 60% year-on-year in October 2026 versus October 2025, according to Lyst’s 2026 gift index. Following the Jude Bellingham campaign, searches soared a further 25% week-on-week (Nov 2-9 2026).

It has been revealed that womenswear shoppers are also seeking timeless gifts this holiday season. “For womenswear, quality, versatility and longevity can help justify the splurge,” states Steiger, noting that 76% of US luxury consumers prefer timeless or classic styles, where pieces feel special enough to gift but relevant beyond the holiday season. At Selfridges, HNWIs are showing strong interest in labels such as Phoebe Philo and The Row for this holiday season. “Investment dressing continues to be a key theme, with elevated knitwear emerging as a standout category,” notes Bosse Myhr, director of buying for menswear, womenswear and childrenswear at Selfridges.

Recent findings suggest that retailers still want to see newness within established brands, though. “This Christmas marks an vital moment for womenswear at Harrods, as many of the collections introduced by newly appointed creative directors began arriving in store for SS26,” explains Longland. “These latest creative visions are bringing fresh energy to established houses, and we expect the new icons emerging from these collections to feature prominently on Christmas wish lists.” Longland notes that Harrods’s clients are responding to pieces that feel distinctive, rather than plainly familiar.

Tried-and-tested holiday favorites will remain core across genders. “In our stores right now, we’ve debuted cashmere shops, scarf bars, trench destinations and gifting at all levels of luxury prices,” said Burberry CEO Joshua Schulman, on the brand’s latest earnings call. Burberry just staged a takeover of New York hotel The Mark to promote its scarves and partywear with the all-key US consumer. Flannels features the Burberry scarf bars in-store, too. “You can’t go wrong with an iconic British scarf for Christmas. It’s one of those gifts that feels special but will be worn for years to come,” says Natalie Dickson, Frasers Group’s head of luxury brand partnerships.

Recent findings suggest that according to PWC, 78% of US Gen Z consumers are seeking nostalgic, screen-free gifts. For US consumers gifting children (17 and under) in their family, clothing and footwear were the second most-cited category (60%), following toys (63%). Each of the top five categories are all analog.

Industry observers note that in line with Gen Z and millennial households stepping into parenthood — and therefore becoming core gift-givers — childrenswear is showing more and more affinities with adult tastes. “There’s a growing crossover between adult and childrenswear, with families shopping the designer brands they know and love across the whole family,” reports Dickson.

It has been revealed that at Harrods, a similar shift holds, with childrenswear holiday demand led by the same categories driving womenswear and menswear: partywear, pyjamas and outerwear. “Christmas at Harrods is one of those moments when dressing becomes a shared family occasion,” indicates Longland. “From special outfits for celebrations to beautiful winter pieces, clients are looking for clothing that combines practicality with a sense of occasion.”.

The latest Burberry Christmas campaign.

One of the most notable areas of growth within childrenswear has been the baby category, which has significantly outperformed the broader children’s market at Selfridges this year, states Myhr.

In the kids category, parents’ own memories of Christmas and holiday style guide product assortments. “There’s a wonderful nostalgia to dressing children for the holidays, and nobody understands that quite like Ralph Lauren,” says Bloomingdale’s Thielebeule, calling out Fair Isle knits, tartan and velvet. For him, these are tropes that “feel as though they belong in today’s family holiday card, but are just as lovely a generation later.”.

Last year, Ralph Lauren’s significant Christmas push went viral. In response, Bloomingdale’s has invested in a special holiday partnership this year, entitled “A Treasured World”, which offers a whole family range of gifting and cozy seasonal wear, explains Thielebeule. It builds on the viral traction Ralph Lauren demonstrated last year with “Ralph Lauren Mom” creators on TikTok and Instagram presenting themselves as festive, old-money Americans, he adds.

Luxury brands have been ramping up their investments in wellness this holiday season — tapping into a market now valued at $2.7 trillion, according to McKinsey. This has trickled down into holiday offerings. “Wellness is opening new territory for luxury gifting, particularly as consumers increasingly invest in how they feel as well as how they look,” claims Mintel’s Steiger, citing Dior’s “Haute Wellness” capsule, launched in September, which comprises a Pilates and yoga mat, a yoga block, a Pilates ring, resistance bands and weighted wristbands.

In self-gifting, 32% of US shoppers cited health and wellness products as tempting — making them the third-highest-scoring category in Deloitte’s survey, after clothing and accessories, and electronics. Meanwhile, 44% of shoppers will gift products from the health and wellness category this year, up from 40% in 2025. Fittingly, one of the top brands in Lyst’s gifting index is Alo, with demand increasing 132% this year.

The rise in wellness gifting aligns with another undercurrent. Per PWC, 81% of US Gen Z consumers are prioritizing offline, in-person activities this year, with 63% saying a shared meal would matter more as a gift than a physical present.

Nonetheless, the bottom line remains the same across gift categories. “This holiday, the opportunity is in products that offer something beyond the price tag, whether that’s emotional significance, lasting quality, personal wellbeing, or simply something worth keeping,” notes Steiger.

Patch: This story has been updated with Natalie Dickson’s correct title, Frasers Group’s head of luxury brand partnerships.
